title: Performance, price, and speed across model tiers

opening.headline: When requirements are numerous and there is no basis for determining which model grade is appropriate, selection criteria are established based on the trade-offs among performance, price, and speed.
body: When applying generative AI to a service, the first question you'll encounter is which model to use. It's easy to choose among well-known models, models that perform well in demos, or models you've tried before, but such choices can lead to subpar quality or excessive costs and delays.

In this class, we confirm that the model product lines of three companies are arranged along a single ladder, ranging from small and fast to large and powerful. After learning how to compare ratings using the same criteria, we apply this approach to three tasks: customer inquiry classification, contract review, and image description.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the trade-offs among performance, price, and speed by model tier.
Can analyze the appropriate starting grade by matching business requirements with grade-specific characteristics.

screens.title: The requirements are numerous, but there is no basis for selecting a grade.
screens.lead: First, read about a common scenario you'll encounter when planning a service. Think about what aspect is blocked while reading.

visual.alt: A scene showing six separate requirement cards scattered on the left, and a model grade ladder marked with question marks on the right.

paragraphs: A team is building an internal service. Six requirements have accumulated. The system must classify customer inquiries, review contracts, and describe images. Responses must return within two seconds, monthly costs must stay within a limit, and errors must be rare.

Looking at the product lineup, there are three tiers: the smallest, the medium, and the largest. However, there is no basis for determining which of the six requirements should be placed in which tier. Without such justification, selecting any tier risks one of two failures: choosing a tier that is too small results in insufficient quality, while choosing a tier that is too large leads to excessive cost and delay.

Upon closer examination, the six requirements ultimately fall into three categories: how accurate they must be (quality), how usable they must be (cost), and how fast they must be (speed). This course addresses how to divide requirements into these three axes and examines how they differ across various levels of grading.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are the three conditions—response in under 2 seconds, monthly cost cap, and rare errors—pointing in the same direction or do they clash with each other? We'll revisit this question at the end of the class.

screens.outro: Now, think back to how you selected the model in this service.

screens.title: Recall the rationale for selecting a service model currently in use
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought summary is displayed. Please first mentally consider the answer before clicking.

items.prompt: What criteria were used to select the model for the current service?
items.answer: Common justifications are four: first, because it is well known; second, because it is frequently demonstrated; third, because it uses the original model unchanged; and fourth, by dividing requirements into numerical values for analysis. The first three reasons are difficult to serve as valid justification, while only the last one provides a basis that can be re-examined and revised. This course focuses on the process of developing the last approach.

items.prompt: If we are still using the original model unchanged, is that model larger than or smaller than the requirements?
items.answer: Most respond that they have never verified this. With a large model, quality may be sufficient, but additional costs and delays could be incurred; with a smaller model, error costs might be incurred instead. Either way, it's impossible to determine without first assessing the complexity of the requirements and the acceptable delay.

items.prompt: Have you ever thought about ways to adjust quality and cost instead of replacing the model?
items.answer: Yes. An example is a setting that adjusts inference strength within the same model. The Claude documentation advises that it is often better to adjust the effort parameter rather than switching models, as it balances intelligence with latency and cost within a single model. The following screen revisits this feature.

screens.outro: Let's first check what grade means across the product lines of three companies.

screens.title: Model tier refers to: a ladder within a product family
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the grade structures by company. Note that although the names may differ, the structures are the same.

visual.alt: A diagram showing three companies' rating ladders placed side by side vertically, with increasing capability as you go upward.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude is composed of four tiers. **Haiku 5.5** is the fastest tier, designed for high-throughput, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing. **Sonnet 5.5** is a faster tier that balances speed and intelligence. **Opus 55** is designed for long-running agent-based coding and knowledge work. **Fable 5.1** is the slowest tier, intended for complex reasoning and long-term agent tasks. All four models support text and image inputs as well as tool usage.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI has three tiers. **Luna** is an efficient tier suited for defined tasks, categorization, and frequently recurring automation. **GPT-6.1 Sol** is a mid-tier designed for complex tasks that also require time and cost management. **Astra** is the top-tier for ambiguous problems, deep analysis, and ambitious outputs. The document introduces Luna as the most cost-effective model and Astra as the most powerful model.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: The Gemini product line also follows the same structure. **Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite** is the fastest and most cost-effective tier, suitable for high-throughput tasks. **Gemini 3.8 Flash** is a mid-tier designed for long-term coding and agent workflows, as well as complex tasks. **Gemini 4 Argon** is the flagship reasoning model, intended for tasks requiring deep reasoning.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body: All three companies are arranged along a single line, from small and weak to large and strong. The small side is fast and inexpensive, making it suitable for narrow tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing; the large side is slow and costly, but suited for ambiguous and complex tasks. Therefore, you don't need to remember the grade names. As long as you know which one is the smallest and which one is the largest, you can understand them in the same way.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the structure, we'll now examine numerically what is being swapped between grades.

screens.title: Presenting the trade-offs among performance, price, and speed in a single table
screens.lead: Move the slider to switch between Claude grades from Haiku 5.5 to Fable 5.1. Each time the value changes, the speed, price, and limit for that grade are displayed.

visual.alt: A chart displaying the Claude grade input prices side by side in a bar format.
labels: Quality capability increases over time, and so do price and delay.

stops.body: It is the fastest. Pricing starts at $0.10 per input MTok and $0.50 per output MTok, based on prompts under 100K tokens. Context window is 1M tokens, with a maximum output of 128K tokens. The default effort level is medium. It serves as a starting point for tasks involving frequent calls and latency-sensitive operations such as classification, extraction, and routing.

The speed is fast. The pricing is $2 per input MTok and $10 per output MTok. The context window is 1M tokens, with a maximum output of 128K tokens, matching Haiku. The default effort level is high. It offers a good balance between speed and intelligence, serving as a benchmark when deciding between the two extremes.

The speed is average. The pricing is $4 per input MTok and $20 per output MTok. The context window is 1M tokens, with a maximum output of 128K tokens, and the default effort level is medium. When it's unclear which model to use, the guidance recommends starting with Opus 5.5 for most tasks. It is well-suited for long-agent coding and knowledge-intensive workloads.

The speed is slow. The pricing is $10 per input MTok and $50 per output MTok, the highest among the five tiers. The context window is 1M tokens, with a maximum output of 128K tokens. This tier is intended for challenging inference and long-term agent tasks, or when evaluating Opus 5.5 with high effort remains insufficient.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the conflicts between the grades, let's now review the selection guidelines for the three companies using the same criteria.

data.notes: The commonality among the three guides is that they both use two handles: one is the model tier and the other is the inference strength. Regardless of which side you start from, the flow of increasing or decreasing results after verification is the same.

screens.outro: Since you've learned how to read the benchmarks, let's move on to a case study illustrating how to map requirements to their corresponding grade levels.

screens.title: Explanation of Grade Selection for Three Tasks
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates sequentially selecting the grade for each of the three tasks. Use the right arrow to advance step by step and follow the decision process.

steps.title: Common procedure: First write down the difficulty and allowable delay.
steps.body: Before addressing the three tasks, establish an order. First, record the required difficulty, allowable delay, and error cost for each task. Next, choose between efficiency-first and capability-first as the starting point, then adjust upward or downward based on the results. The values below are assumptions for illustrative purposes; you must replace them with actual values based on your requirements.

steps.title: Task 1: Customer Inquiry Classification: Start from low tier
steps.body: The input is short with high daily call volume and must respond within two seconds. As a narrow-range classification task, the difficulty is low, with latency and cost being the primary constraints. Therefore, we start with the smallest models such as Haiku 5.5, Luna, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. We only increase the model size by one tier if cases are found where classification accuracy falls below the benchmark.

steps.title: Task 2. Contract Review: Start from higher tier
steps.body: Contracts involve high costs from a single error and require analyzing relationships between clauses to infer meaning. Accuracy should take precedence over delay, so start with higher-tier versions like Opus 5.5, increasing effort accordingly. If results sufficiently exceed benchmarks, reduce effort or downgrade to a lower tier to cut costs. It is generally better to first adjust effort rather than replace the model.

steps.title: Task 3. Image Description: Determine difficulty after confirming input support.
steps.body: When evaluating image descriptions, first verify whether the model accepts image input. According to the Claude documentation, all current models support both text and image inputs, so this criterion does not affect the rating. The remaining criterion is the difficulty of the description. If the task involves describing the objects in an image in one sentence, a lower rating is sufficient. However, if the task requires explaining the relationships within a diagram, it is safer to start one level higher.

steps.title: Summary: Three tasks and selected departure class
steps.body: Customer inquiry classification is dominated by delay and call volume, so it is assigned the lowest priority; contract review is dominated by error costs, thus assigned a higher priority with greater effort; image description is assigned intermediate priority, depending on difficulty after confirming input support. All three tasks share the commonality of first specifying difficulty and allowable delay before assigning priority. This represents the rule mapping from requirements to priority levels.

screens.outro: I will once again summarize the procedures selected from these three cases on the final screen.

screens.title: From requirement to grade: process consolidation
screens.lead: Let's summarize the content covered in this class into a single procedure. Please answer the questions again as posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Model selection starts with requirements, not with names. First, list the difficulty of the work, allowable delay, error cost, and monthly cost ceiling. By examining how these four factors align within the three axes of quality, cost, and speed, you begin to identify where to start.

Ratings are ladders where the axes are mutually inverted. Lower ratings are fast and cheap but weak in complex reasoning, while higher ratings are slower and more expensive, offering greater capability. All three companies use the same architecture; Claude's five ratings have identical context windows of 1M tokens and maximum outputs of 128K tokens, differing primarily in reasoning capability, speed, and price.

The starting point is either efficiency-first or capability-first, and it is adjusted up or down based on the results. Aside from grade, another lever is the strength of inference such as effort, which can be tuned before switching models. When returning to the initial question, response speed, cost ceiling, and low error rate are mutually conflicting conditions, and their balance directly corresponds to the combination of grade and effort.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The prices and limits in the text are based on the Claude benchmark values specified in the document, and the numerical values by task are assumptions for illustrative purposes. To make actual selections, simply state your own requirements in the same manner, and then adjust the ratings and effort levels based on the resulting outcomes.

glossary.def: These are model stages within a product line ordered by increasing capability. The smaller models are faster and more affordable, while the larger models offer greater capability.
This is inference strength configuration that allows trading off intelligence against latency and cost within the same model.
A unit denoting one million tokens, serving as the basis for determining the per-input and per-output pricing in model pricing.
A procedure to determine the appropriate grade by noting the difficulty of the task, allowable delay, and error cost.

misconceptions.myth: The largest model is always the best.
misconceptions.fact: Tasks with narrow scopes such as classification or extraction often have smaller grades that are faster, cheaper, and sufficient. Larger grades are typically used for ambiguous and difficult tasks.

misconceptions.myth: If the grades are different, the context size is also greatly different.
misconceptions.fact: The current Claude tier levels all have a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens. The differences mainly lie in reasoning capability, speed, and price.

misconceptions.myth: To improve quality, you must change the model.
misconceptions.fact: Adjusting effort settings often provides a better handle than switching models. The Claude documentation also recommends adjusting effort before changing models.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Model selection starts with the complexity of the requirements and the allowable delay.
Grade is a ladder where performance, price, and speed trade off against each other, and all three companies use the same architecture.
Start with efficiency or capacity-based benchmarks, and adjust up or down based on shortages or excesses.
In addition to grade, inference strength factors like effort are also handles for cost and delay.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
